LM Information Technology Specialist Kyle Brown accepted the award on LM’s behalf. The EPEAT award recognizes organizations for excellence in sustainable procurement of electronic equipment. EPEAT is a method for purchasers to evaluate a product’s effect on the environment, rate it accordingly, and identify it as a preferable electronic good. Manufacturers register products in the EPEAT category based on the device’s ability to meet certain criteria, including product lifestyle, design, energy production, and recycling. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Legacy Management (LM) recently welcomed Michelle Scott to the LM Financial Audits and Contract Services team. Scott, who previously worked with the LM Support Partner (LMSP), transitioned to the LM side in September. “I’m so excited to transition to the federal side of the LM contract,” Scott said. “I’ve really enjoyed working with everyone on the contracting team, and I’m grateful to be able to start this new journey.” After attending West Virginia University, Scott worked as a realtor before starting with LMSP. Scott worked for LMSP for more than 18 years, assisting to build and execute multiple integrated master schedules and specializing in analyzing complex scopes, schedules, and budget forecasting to uncover efficiencies. pages.text: Lobito Corridor: Can Trump-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo and Angola? Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Weather Newsletters Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo? 3 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Akisa Wandera BBC Africa, Lobito AFP via Getty Images The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments. She is thinking about getting around more easily. The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast. For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient. "Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says. But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport. It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo. Long COVID Basics For Everyone May 6, 2026 Español Key points Long COVID is a serious illness that can result in chronic conditions, require comprehensive care, and can sometimes cause disability. Long COVID can include a wide range of ongoing symptoms and conditions that can last months to years after COVID-19 illness. Anyone who had a SARS-CoV-2 infection, the virus that causes COVID-19, can experience Long COVID, including children. Following core strategies to lower your risk of severe COVID-19 illness is the best way to prevent Long COVID. Living with Long COVID can be difficult and isolating, especially when there are no approved tests that can determine if your symptoms or conditions are due to Long COVID and there are no approved treatments. About Long COVID Long COVID is defined as a chronic condition that occurs after SARS-CoV-2 infection and is present for at least 3 months. Long COVID includes a wide range of symptoms or conditions that may improve, worsen, or be ongoing. Talk to your healthcare provider if you have symptoms that last for months after an infection. Long-Duration Energy Storage Background From providing critical backup power during natural disasters to supporting more renewable energy coming online, energy storage technologies make the grid more flexible and resilient. Today’s energy storage technologies are not sufficiently scaled or affordable enough to meet energy demand that fluctuates throughout the day and night. Long-duration energy storage (LDES) is a cost-effective option to increase grid reliability and resilience so that reliable, affordable electricity is available whenever and wherever to everyone. DOE defines LDES as storage systems capable of delivering electricity for 10 or more hours in duration. Program Overview The Long-Duration Energy Storage portfolio helps to advance LDES systems toward widespread commercial deployment. The goal of this portfolio is to fund projects that will overcome the technical and institutional barriers that exist for deployment, with a focus on different technology types for a diverse set of regions. But in August, three exceptionally bright stars offer an easy starting point. Vega, Deneb, and Altair form the Summer Triangle, an enormous star pattern that rises high in the evening sky across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Once you find it, the triangle can serve as a guide to nearby constellations, deep-sky objects, and the Milky Way. It is also one of the most photogenic regions of the summer sky in August. Here’s how to find the Summer Triangle—and photograph what surrounds it. How to Find the Summer Triangle The Summer Triangle is not a constellation, but an asterism, or a recognizable pattern of stars. Begin with Vega, one of the brightest stars visible from Earth. In mid-August, observers in the Northern Hemisphere can generally find it high overhead. Deneb appears to one side of Vega, while Altair lies farther away, creating a large, elongated triangle. Here's why it happens and where to look. Venus, the Pleiades star cluster, and the bright star Capella rise in the dawn sky above a tufa formation in California’s Mono Lake. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published November 12, 2026 Look low in the northeastern sky on an autumn evening, and you might spot something unusual: a bright star flashing red, green, and blue. That’s Capella, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. But despite appearances, the star isn’t actually changing colors. The dazzling display is an optical effect caused by starlight passing through Earth’s atmosphere. And Capella isn’t the only star that puts on this kind of show. “Stars appear to twinkle or shimmer in the night sky, but this is not an inherent trait of stars,” says Emily Watson, astrophysicist and planetarium supervisor at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center. “As the light from a star passes through different densities and temperatures within our atmosphere, the light bends in a process called refraction.” The color flashes happen because Earth’s atmosphere bends different wavelengths of light by different degrees. pages.text: Looking for whales—and awe—in Baja California | National Geographic TRAVEL Looking for whales—and awe—in Baja California The Gulf of California was once known as “the aquarium of the world.” But on a recent whale watching trip—and in an era where climate change is making its mark—our writer wonders if it still delivers. The Sea of Cortez is famous for its marine mammals, including fin, minke, humpback whales, seals, and sea lions, as well as common and bottlenose dolphins. Story and video by Kinsey Gidick Published May 15, 2026 When considering a trip to Baja, it’s nearly impossible to dodge the words of two famous men: Jacques Cousteau and John Steinbeck. The pioneering French oceanographer famously called the Gulf of California “the aquarium of the world.” Not surprisingly, that line shows up everywhere—typed into brochures and slipped into itineraries, hovering like a promise. Meanwhile, Steinbeck’s The Log from the Sea of Cortez , the Pulitzer winner’s account of his 1940 six-week, 4,000-mile expedition examining tide pools and collecting specimens along the narrow sea is practically required reading. To be fair, the acclaim is well earned. Steinbeck’s account reads like a dispatch from another, more poetic, planet. But these touchstones sketched a vision of abundance so vivid, especially in a climate-anxious age, that they almost felt like fables: beautiful, sure, yet just distant enough to raise my eyebrow. Originally born from Afro-Colombian communities, cumbia spread across the Spanish-speaking world , acquiring distinct musical accents along the way. In Peru, cumbia became particularly popular among oil workers deep in the Amazon. And when Jorge Rodriguez Grández started Los Mirlos in his small hometown of Moyobamba, his band played a regional style called cumbia amazónica, easily identifiable by its electric, reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Sponsor Message Alt.Latino Cumbia: The Musical Backbone Of Latin America Los Mirlos' time behind the Desk is not only a joyful celebration of this music but also a trail of small towns and cities throughout the Amazon jungle. Throughout their performance, these cultural ambassadors share stories and declare their love for cumbia and their tropical homeland. We are so fortunate to host and share with you a group of true pioneers and innovators who, over 50 years later, still effortlessly pump out cumbia grooves. pages.text: Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino Last week we published a Tiny Desk Concert that ended up being unusual for a few reasons. First of all, it was the final production of our sixth annual El Tiny series. This was a very emotional moment for a lot of reasons. People really love Los Tigres del Norte, to the point that playing their albums feels like sitting with family. And if you’ve seen the introduction I gave the band just before they played at the desk you can see that I wasn’t embarrassed to get emotional when I talked about what the band means to me. That emotional intro led to some changes in our process and format that resulted in a huge response from the audience that went viral. The result was a messy moment behind the scenes here at NPR and more than a little confusion for a lot of you. This week’s episode looks back at last week. First we want to share with you, directly from us, an explanation of what happened. But mostly we want to put the spotlight back on the band and their music because for decades they have been bringing out the kind emotions that got this whole thing started. Classic car tours are the pinnacle of slow-lane luxury, with vintage vehicles and cinematic roads to choose from. Photograph by Turo By Connor McGovern Published November 15, 2025 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Nothing beats hitting the open road. There’s something undeniably romantic about watching a destination roll by — all on your own schedule — and if you’ve opted for a convertible, the age-old cliche of feeling ‘the wind in your hair’ can become an exhilarating reality. Trend reports from the likes of Travelbag and Travel Tomorrow cite ‘slow travel’ as an enduring trend this year, where travellers take things a little more leisurely, focusing on the quality and depth of experiences rather than ticking off a list. pages.text: Luxor's Temples Will Fall Into Darkness for Six Minutes During the 2027 Eclipse | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD In 2027, See Luxor in a New Light In addition to the total eclipse that will cast the ancient city in shadow, new hotels and other experiences offer fresh incentive to visit the sphinxes and temples on the banks of the Nile. In the early morning hours outside Luxor, it is common to see dozens of hot-air balloons carrying visitors above ongoing excavation work near the Hungarian Archeological Mission in Thebes. András Zoltai By Zoey Goto Published October 20, 2026 The six-minute “eclipse of the century” in August 2027 will bring an influx of astrotourists to Luxor, but the city has far more to offer than any single celestial event. Straddling both banks of the Nile, Egypt's ancient capital is entering a new chapter, with a host of high-profile openings and experiences to complement its Pharaonic wonders. The lavishly restored Mandarin Oriental Winter Palace and the new Four Seasons Hotel Luxor are both set to welcome guests next year. Also making its debut is the 80-passenger Guardian of the Nile, Egypt's first luxury tourist sleeper train, which will stop in Luxor on its way from Cairo to Aswan. Tour the 3,000-year-old temples of Karnak, then soar above them in a hot-air balloon. pages.text: Mammals Made By Viruses | National Geographic SCIENCE THE LOOM Mammals Made By Viruses By Carl Zimmer Published February 14, 2012 • 6 min read If not for a virus, none of us would ever be born. In 2000, a team of Boston scientists discovered a peculiar gene in the human genome. It encoded a protein made only by cells in the placenta. They called it syncytin. The cells that made syncytin were located only where the placenta made contact with the uterus. They fuse together to create a single cellular layer, called the syncytiotrophoblast, which is essential to a fetus for drawing nutrients from its mother. The scientists discovered that in order to fuse together, the cells must first make syncytin. What made syncytin peculiar was that it was not a human gene. It bore all the hallmarks of a gene from a virus. Viruses have insinuated themselves into the genome of our ancestors for hundreds of millions of years. They typically have gotten there by infecting eggs or sperm, inserting their own DNA into ours. There are 100,000 known fragments of viruses in the human genome, making up over 8% of our DNA. Most of this virus DNA has been hit by so many mutations that it’s nothing but baggage our species carries along from one generation to the next. Yet there are some viral genes that still make proteins in our bodies. Syncytin appeared to be a hugely important one to our own biology. From Fort Benton to the Charles M. Russell National Wildlife Refuge, the monument spans 149 miles of the Upper Missouri River and encompasses 377,000 acres of adjacent Breaks country, including portions of Arrow Creek, Antelope Creek, and the Judith River. The monument includes six wilderness study areas, the Cow Creek Area of Critical Environmental Concern, segments of the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail and the Nez Perce National Historic Trail, the Fort Benton National Historic Landmark, a watchable wildlife area, and the Missouri Breaks Back Country Byway. In 1976, Congress designated the Missouri River segment and corridor in this area a National Wild and Scenic River. In some areas, the BLM lands are intermingled with State of Montana lands and private property. The monument designation applies only to the BLM-managed lands. Often called “sea cows” because of their grazing habits, these gentle giants can grow to more than 10 feet long and weigh over 1,000 pounds. Despite their impressive size, manatees are peaceful, slow-moving animals that spend much of their time feeding on aquatic vegetation, resting, and traveling through coastal waters, rivers, estuaries, and springs. West Indian manatees swim in the clear, shallow waters of the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area in Jupiter, Florida. The Bureau of Land Management site is the only BLM-managed area where manatees are regularly observed and provides important habitat for these gentle marine mammals. pages.text: Manchester City charges: Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if sponsors sue - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Manchester City have won the Premier League on eight occasions By Dan Roan Sports editor Published 33 minutes ago Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors if any of Manchester City 's sponsors sue them. The clubs met in London on Thursday for the first time since City were found guilty of a catalogue of charges relating to the breaching of financial rules by an independent commission. City have appealed, with a sanction yet to be decided. The club's sponsors Etihad and Etisalat have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League. But the league's rules will now be amended to provide legal indemnity for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittan and three other non-executive directors. Sources have told BBC Sport that City were one of two Premier League clubs that voted against the amendment, with the other 18 clubs voting in favour. An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenues by over £830m over a nine-year period in September. The commission determined that the club arranged "sham" contracts with sponsors, which disguised funding from club owners the Abu Dhabi United Group. Premier League CEO Masters said City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade". Treasures of the Globally Popular Japanese Comic Book Medium Are on View in New York Skip to main content The first rooms of the "Art of Manga" exhibition introduce visitors to manga, which is read right-to-left and usually published in black and white. Paula Abreu Pita Manga are Japanese comic books and graphic novels. They are typically written and illustrated by a single person, known as mangaka . They are usually printed in black and white and read right-to-left. And they are incredibly popular, in Japan and beyond. When Frederik L. Schodt, author of Manga! Manga! The World of Japanese Comics , published his book in the 1980s, “almost no one in the United States knew what manga was,” he tells the New York Times ’ Shivani Vora. Things have changed. Manga’s popularity is booming in the United States. “Today, young Americans have no problem with manga at all,” he says. “They are happy to read them Japanese-style, turning pages and viewing panels right-to-left.” More than 40 percent of Gen Z watches anime shows, which are often adaptations of manga, compared to just 25 percent who follow professional football. Now, the illustrated medium and its most well-known mangaka are the centerpiece of a new exhibition at the Brooklyn Museum in New York. “ Art of Manga ” is the country’s first large-scale show to explore the art form’s evolution, individual voices and cross-cultural impact. “The show’s focus on artists is what makes it so special.
